opus-5.5.text:
I think of it a bit like the difference between a brilliant generalist collaborator and a very precise instrument in the lab. Both matter, but they do different jobs.

General models, the large language models, are good at the "thinking around the experiment" part. They've absorbed a huge amount of literature across fields, so they can help you frame a hypothesis, connect an idea from materials science to a problem in biology, suggest controls you forgot, or draft a protocol. They're good at reasoning in language, at planning, at asking "what if." But they're not reliable at the quantitative core. If you ask a general model to predict a protein's binding affinity or the yield of a reaction, it might give you a confident-sounding number that's basically a guess.

Specialized models are the opposite. Something like a protein structure predictor, a molecular property model, or a surrogate model trained on a specific family of experiments is narrow, but within its domain it's grounded in real data and physical constraints. It can screen thousands or millions of candidates and tell you which few are worth making. It doesn't know why you're asking, and it can't redesign the study, but its answer is something you can actually trust and test.

So in practice I see them working as a stack. The general model acts as the orchestrator, or the "PI's assistant": it reads the literature, proposes directions, decides which tools to call, and interprets results in context. The specialized models are the tools it calls: predict this structure, score these molecules, optimize these reaction conditions. Then the real experiment, often automated in a self-driving lab, closes the loop, and the data flows back to improve the specialized models.

The mistake I see is people expecting one to replace the other. A general model alone hallucinates in the details; a specialized model alone can't tell you whether you're asking the right question. The interesting science happens when you combine the breadth of one with the precision of the other, and keep a human scientist in the loop to judge what's actually meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the cleanest way to put it is that specialized models and general models sit at different layers of the experimental loop, and the mistake people make is asking one to do the other's job.

Specialized models are, at their core, very good function approximators for a narrow physical question. Something like AlphaFold for protein structure, or a model trained on density functional theory data to predict formation energies, or a model that predicts whether a given synthesis recipe will actually produce a stable crystal. They're fast, they're quantitative, and within their training distribution they can be remarkably accurate. But they have no idea why you're asking. You hand them an input and they hand you a number. They don't know what question you're trying to answer, they don't know that the last three experiments failed, and they don't know that your lab doesn't have a glovebox.

General models are the opposite. They're not great at predicting a band gap to two decimal places, and you shouldn't trust them to be. But they can read the literature, hold the context of the project, reason about what a result means, and decide what to try next. In the experimental design sense, they do the thing a good graduate student or a good PI does. They form hypotheses, they weigh tradeoffs, they notice that two papers disagree, and they figure out which specialized tool to call to resolve the disagreement.

So the way I think about it in practice: the general model is the planner and the orchestrator, and the specialized models are instruments. The general model proposes a space of candidate materials, calls a specialized model to screen ten thousand of them for stability, calls another one to estimate synthesizability, looks at the ranked list, and then uses judgment about which handful actually go to the robot or the bench. After the experiment runs, it reads the characterization data, compares it to what the specialized models predicted, and updates the plan.

What's important is that the loop closes. The specialized models are only as good as their training data, and real experiments are where the training distribution gets stretched. So the general model's job isn't just to use the tools, it's to notice when the tools are wrong. When the predicted phase doesn't show up in the XRD, that discrepancy is actually the most valuable thing you learned that day, and a general model can recognize it as such, whereas a specialized model will just keep confidently predicting the same thing.

There's one more distinction I'd add. Specialized models encode physics. General models encode scientific practice. The physics part changes slowly and benefits from being learned precisely. The practice part is messy, full of tacit knowledge, and changes with every project. I don't think you want to merge those into one system. You want a general reasoner that knows how to use a toolbox of precise, narrow instruments, and that knows the limits of each one.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish them by the kind of problem they solve. A specialized model focuses on a relatively narrow scientific task—predicting a property of a molecule, for example. A general model can help connect that task to the broader experimental process: What are we trying to discover? What evidence do we already have? Which experiment would help distinguish between competing explanations?

So they’re complementary. The general model can help formulate a hypothesis and identify which tools are needed; a specialized model can make predictions within its domain. Those predictions can then inform the experimental design, including controls and measurements.

But designing an experiment isn’t just about finding something likely to succeed. Sometimes the most valuable experiment is the one that reduces uncertainty. Neither type of model replaces experimental validation or the scientist’s judgment about what the results actually establish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between depth in a particular domain and the ability to coordinate the whole experiment. A specialized model might predict a protein’s structure, estimate a material’s properties, or simulate a physical process. It gives you a powerful capability within a relatively well-defined problem.

A general model can help connect those capabilities. Given a scientific question, it might help formulate hypotheses, identify which specialized models to call, propose an experimental workflow, and interpret the results in context. So I see the two as complementary: the general model helps organize the investigation, while specialized models provide depth where it matters.

But proposing an experiment is different from establishing that it will work. You still need to account for uncertainty, physical constraints, available equipment, and whether the result actually distinguishes between competing hypotheses. Ultimately, the experiment has to provide the evidence.
